messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Meet 25-year-old Jamal, a housekeeper who has been struggling to come to terms with his traumatic past. As a child, Jamal suffered physical abuse at the hands of his caregiver, an experience that has left an indelible mark on his life. Jamal's days are often marked by a sense of hypervigilance, as if he is constantly on guard against potential threats. He can't shake off the feeling that others can see right through him, that they know about the abuse just by looking at him. This feeling of exposure makes him want to escape, to drift off into his own world where he feels safe. Jamal has developed a coping mechanism - fantasy escape - where he detaches himself from reality and enters a world of his own creation. But this escape is short-lived. The slightest trigger can transport him back to the traumatic event. The sound of children crying, for instance, is enough to set off a chain reaction. Jamal's mind starts racing, and he feels like he's reliving the experience all over again. The memories come flooding back - vivid, full sensory replays that leave him feeling overwhelmed and helpless. When these memories resurface, Jamal tries to give up important responsibilities, hoping to avoid triggers and stay safe. He'll call in sick or abandon tasks halfway through, unable to shake off the feeling of impending doom. His colleagues have noticed this pattern, but Jamal can't explain why he's been so unreliable lately. All he knows is that he needs to escape, to find a way out of the darkness that seems to be closing in on him. As the memories replay in his mind, Jamal starts to feel like an object, not a person. He's convinced that others see him as damaged goods, someone who can never truly be whole again. This dehumanization makes him more withdrawn, more determined to avoid human contact at all costs. Never alone is his new mantra - he'll do whatever it takes to ensure that he's always surrounded by people, even if it means sacrificing his own needs and desires. But this strategy backfires. The more Jamal tries to escape, the more memories resurface. And with each replay, the triggers become more potent, more likely to set off a chain reaction of flashbacks and physical reactivity. It's as if his body is constantly on high alert, waiting for the next threat to emerge. As Jamal navigates this complex web of emotions, he becomes increasingly isolated. His relationships suffer, his work performance declines, and he starts to lose touch with reality. The memories continue to haunt him, replaying like a film that refuses to end. And at the center of it all is the feeling of fear - the certainty that harm can come from anywhere, at any time. It's this sense of hopelessness that finally brings Jamal to seek help. He's exhausted by the constant struggle, the endless cycle of triggers and memories and maladaptive strategies. As he sits in the therapist's office, he knows that he needs to confront his demons head-on. It won't be easy - but for the first time in years, Jamal feels a glimmer of hope. Maybe, just maybe, he can learn to overcome his past and find a way forward.
